e-5299.knowledge_point: Calculating the Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function
e-5299.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x .$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=\frac{1}{(x+2)(x-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)(x-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the two solutions $x = -2$ and $x = 3.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x = -2$ and $x = 3.$

e-5302.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes With Common Factors in the Numerator and Denominator
e-5302.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-6x+8} \\  & =\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x-2}}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x-4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x - 4 = 0
$$

This gives the solution $x = 4.$ Therefore, $x = 4$ is the only vertical asymptote.

e-5301.problem: Find the vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^3+x^2+4x}.$
e-5301.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+4x} \\  & =\frac{2}{x({x}^{2}+x+4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
x(x^2 +x+ 4) = 0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $x = 0$ gives the solution $x = 0.$

- The equation $x^2 +x+ 4 = 0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $\mathcal D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(1{)}^{2}-4(1)(4) \\  & =1-16 \\  & =-15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x = 0.$

e-5304.problem: Determine the vertical asymptotes of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2-x-6}{x^3 - 3 x^2 + x - 3}.$
e-5304.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-x-6}{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+x-3} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-3)}{{x}^{2}(x-3)+(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)(x-3)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)\cancel{(x-3)}}{({x}^{2}+1)\cancel{(x-3)}} \\  & =\frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x^2 + 1 = 0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant $\mathcal D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(0{)}^{2}-4(1)(1) \\  & =0-4 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
f(x)=\frac{3}{2(x+2)(x-2)}.
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the two solutions $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)(x+1)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the three solutions $x=-3,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are  $x=-3,\,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+3x-1}{(x-1)(x+5{)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x-1{)}^{3}}{(x-1)(x+5{)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x-1{)}^{2}}{(x-1)(x+5{)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x-1{)}^{2}}{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+5{)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x-1{)}^{2}}{(x+5{)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
(x+5{)}^{2}=0
$$

This gives the solution $x=-5.$ Therefore, $x=-5$ is the only vertical asymptote.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+2}{{x}^{2}+2x} \\  & =\frac{x+2}{x(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x+2}}{x\cancel{(x+2)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
x=0
$$

This gives the solution $x=0.$ Therefore, $x=0$ is the only vertical asymptote.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x} \\  & =\frac{5}{x({x}^{2}+x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
x({x}^{2}+x+1)=0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $2x=0$ gives the solution $x=0.$

- The equation ${x}^{2}+x+1=0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={1}^{2}-4(1)(1) \\  & =1-4 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for x.

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get f(x)=5x3+x2+x=5x(x2+x+1).

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

x(x2+x+1)=0.

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

  • Solving 2x=0 gives the solution x=0.

  • The equation x2+x+1=0 has no real solutions because the discriminant D is negative: D=b2−4ac=12−4(1)(1)=1−4=−3.

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is x=0.

EXPLANATION

To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for x.

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get f(x)=2x−1x3−2x2+4x−8=2x−1x2(x−2)+4(x−2)=2x−1(x2+4)(x−2).

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

(x2+4)(x−2)=0.

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

  • Solving x−2=0 gives the solution x=2.

  • The equation x2+4=0 has no real solutions.

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is x=2.

EXPLANATION

To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for x.

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

f(x)=x2−1x4−1=x2−1(x2−1)(x2+1)=(x−1)(x+1)(x−1)(x+1)(x2+1)=(x−1)(x+1)(x−1)(x+1)(x2+1)=1x2+1

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

x2+1=0 This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, f(x) has no vertical asymptotes.

after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}-6}{{x}^{4}-9} \\  & =\frac{2({x}^{2}-3)}{({x}^{2}-3)({x}^{2}+3)} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{({x}^{2}-3)}}{\cancel{({x}^{2}-3)}({x}^{2}+3)} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+3=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

after.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}({x}^{2}+x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}({x}^{2}+x+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+x+2=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =1-4(1)(2) \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

EXPLANATION

To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for x.

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

f(x)=x2+3xx3+2x2+8x=x(x+3)x(x2+2x+8)=x(x+3)x(x2+2x+8)=x+3x2+2x+8

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

x2+2x+8=0 This equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant D is negative:

D=b2−4ac=22−4(1)(8)=−28

Therefore, f(x) has no vertical asymptotes.

content.problem: Determine the vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+8x}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+8x} \\  & =\frac{x(x+3)}{x({x}^{2}+2x+8)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x}(x+3)}{\cancel{x}({x}^{2}+2x+8)} \\  & =\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+2x+8}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+2x+8=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={2}^{2}-4(1)(8) \\  & =-28\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.
